analysis.one_liner: Caps Medicare drug cost-sharing at the drug's net price after rebates or its pharmacy cash price, whichever is lower.
analysis.headline: Introduced September 8, 2025 with one sponsor and zero cosponsors, the bill sits in two House committees and has had no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets a middleman practice in Medicare's drug benefit: seniors can be charged cost-sharing based on a drug's full list price, even after the plan has received large rebates that bring the drug's real cost down. It would cap what a Medicare beneficiary pays for a covered drug, after the deductible and before reaching the annual out-of-pocket limit, at the drug's average net price (what was actually paid, minus rebates) or the pharmacy's cash price, whichever is lower. It also applies the same cap to copayments for low-income beneficiaries and requires the Government Accountability Office to report on compliance and enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who fill prescriptions after meeting their deductible but before hitting the annual out-of-pocket threshold. Today, their cost-sharing can be calculated off the drug's list price while rebates negotiated behind the scenes never reach them; the bill ties their share to the drug's actual net cost. Low-income beneficiaries get the same protection through a matching copayment cap.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries paying list-price drug copays

how_it_helps.text: For plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2027, cost-sharing for a covered Part D drug dispensed by a pharmacy, for costs above the deductible and before the out-of-pocket threshold, could not exceed the drug's average net price for a month's supply or the pharmacy's applicable cash price, whichever is lower.

Average net price is defined as the average amount actually paid for the drug under the plan, less any rebates or other remuneration the plan receives for it, so rebates must be reflected in what the patient pays.
Copayments for beneficiaries receiving the low-income subsidy are likewise capped at the amount allowed under the new cost-sharing limit, starting in plan year 2027.
The Comptroller General must report to Congress by January 1, 2029 on compliance, enforcement, and ways to improve public awareness of the requirement.

analysis.who_pays: Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers, whose current economics rely on collecting rebates while setting patient cost-sharing off higher list prices, would see that gap shrink. If plans lose cost-sharing revenue faster than rebates offset it, the gap could resurface as higher premiums paid by all beneficiaries and taxpayers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D insurers

drawbacks.text: The cap only covers the middle of the benefit — after the deductible and before the out-of-pocket threshold — so what beneficiaries pay during the deductible phase and the catastrophic phase is unchanged.
Plans would have to base patient cost-sharing on net-of-rebate prices, and any revenue they lose in that middle phase could be shifted into premiums that all Part D enrollees and taxpayers pay.

Using the pharmacy's cash price as a floor adds complexity, since cash prices vary pharmacy by pharmacy, and the bill's own requirement for a GAO report on compliance and enforcement signals that Congress expects monitoring problems.
A plan facing lower cost-sharing revenue on certain drugs could respond by restricting formularies or moving drugs to less favorable tiers, which the bill does not directly prohibit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill takes on a real and widely criticized practice: beneficiaries paying cost-sharing based on list prices while negotiated rebates stay with plans and middlemen. Tying patient cost to the drug's net price is a straightforward fix, and the low-income copayment extension broadens it. But it is a partial fix — it leaves the deductible and catastrophic phases untouched, and the lost plan revenue may resurface in premiums rather than disappearing. On balance it would help seniors who use brand-name drugs in the middle phase of the benefit, with the main cost being possible premium pressure spread across all enrollees.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees, and so far neither has taken it up — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Nicole Malliotakis introduced the bill in the House on September 8, 2025.
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for consideration of provisions falling within each committee's jurisdiction.
The bill has zero cosponsors and no committee action beyond referral has been recorded.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost — the status quo stands. Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D plans continue to set patient cost-sharing off list prices while rebates stay behind the scenes, and beneficiaries continue paying the difference.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no votes have occurred, so no partisan pattern is visible yet.

industries.note: PBMs negotiate rebates that lower a drug's real cost, but patient cost-sharing is commonly set off the higher list price, leaving the spread with middlemen and plans. The bill forces patient cost-sharing down to the net-of-rebate price, directly shrinking that spread. The bill's title itself names 'middlemen' as the target.

Plans keep collecting rebates but would have to set patient cost-sharing at the drug's net price, reducing revenue they currently capture in the middle phase of the benefit. Any lost revenue could reappear as higher premiums charged to all enrollees.

analysis.trajectory: As a single-sponsor bill with no cosponsors, referred to two committees, the realistic path is that it stays in committee and expires at the end of the 119th Congress, as most one-sponsor bills do. It could pick up cosponsors if the rebate-versus-list-price cost-sharing issue gains attention, but that has not happened yet.
